vo.text: Two trains. One track. Heading straight for each other, in the dark.
Neither driver can see the other yet. But both trains start slowing down... and stop, hundreds of meters apart.
Nobody pulled the brake. Something called Kavach did.
Kavach means armour. It's India's own automatic train protection system. Here's how it works.
Step one: the train has to know exactly where it is, even which track it's on. GPS can't tell tracks just a few meters apart.
So small RFID tags are fixed between the rails, about one every kilometer, and at every signal.
A reader under the engine scans each tag as it rolls over it. Exact position. Direction. Which track.
Step two: each station has its own Kavach unit, wired to every signal nearby. It always knows which ones are red.
Radio towers carry that, again and again, to every engine in range.
Step three: the computer on the engine draws a braking curve. At this speed, how far does it need to stop before that red signal?
If the driver doesn't slow down in time, it warns them. And if they still don't act... it brakes by itself.
It enforces speed limits too, and shows the signal right on a screen in the cab, so fog can't hide it.
And if two engines with Kavach end up on the same track, they spot each other, and both stop.
The cost? Roughly fifty lakh rupees per kilometer of track, and about eighty lakh per engine.
By mid twenty twenty-six, Kavach four point oh was live on about twenty-five hundred kilometers of the Delhi to Mumbai and Delhi to Howrah routes. Trackside work covers over twenty thousand more.
Is Kavach on your route yet? Tell me in the comments, and follow for more.
